CAPE TOWN TRANSPORT WAR [6250]

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
..we probe the conflict points in a faceless war on public transport in Cape Town

Unique Selling Point:
We have footage of taxis being impounded in what is arguably the most concentrated and largest law enforcement effort by traffic police in Cape Town to date, setting the scene for a more difficult relationship between the state and the taxi associations who are both operating in a compromised and broken public transport sector. We also will have interview with newly appoint SANTACO provincial head who is attempting to build bridges while on the ground his operators break the rules. As an example of that, we show a case study of an e-hailing entrepreneur whose drivers are regularly stopped by taxi-drivers on a mission to confiscate the cars of competition, or levy a fine, and a letter to transport business owners operating transport from Pollsmoor from CATA threatening to do exactly that in the Tokai area.

Summary:
Public transport related violence flares up monthly in Cape Town, hurting the local economy, undermining freedom of movement on a mass scaled, hurting private and public property and most of all claiming lives. The word on the street is that the taxi associations and operators are intent on driving other forms of public transport off the road - trains, buses, e-hailing, staff and school transport - using violence, intimidation and lawlessness. Now the city is to ratchet up the tension in this low-scale war by introducing a new and unique to the Cape bylaw which will hit the operators where it hurts - in their pockets - while it sets itself up to impound taxi's on an almost industrial scale and not give them back on the same day. In this instance, the Cape is a case-study of extremes, but the head of the Bus Operators Organisation explains that similar scenarios are playing out across the country and we ignore this encroachment at our peril.

Further information:
We will do the interview with Councillor JP Smith, the man leading the state in this low-scale war of regulatory aggression against the taxi sector in the City's pound which is bursting at the scenes with impounded taxis. Beyond the interview, this will give us unique visuals. We also will have access to some of the City's footage of taxi violence.

Extra Budget Items:
We did a shoot in an operation 13 October without a presenter. I will need an extra half day in Johannesburg with Bazil Govender of the Bus Operators Association for an interview and some B-ROll. I am happy to negotiate and carry some of this. We will most likely need to buy some extra taxi violence footage/stills - buses alight - etc but will see what I can get for free first. We did an interview with Jay-Jay Maans after the presenter-let shoot - he was not available at that time.

Press Release:


Slow-burn Transport War / Taking Taxis to Task
A faceless war is raging against competition and regulation in the taxi industry as associations and rogue operators seem intent on running trains, buses, e-hailing, staff and school transport off the road. Threats, intimidation and violence have escalated. Now the City of Cape Town is ratcheting up the tension by introducing a new and unique bylaw which will hit the operators where it hurts – in their pockets. But can the City take back the routes and enforce the law as it impounds taxis on an industrial scale?
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


(VO) It’s 4 am…Cape Town’s traffic police prepare for an early morning swoop on unroadworthy vehicles and illegal taxi operators…it’s a joint operation with the police.

Commanding officer talks to the group:
First of all we have already received information that they are going to attack our vehicles, we already received it last night, and second thing, wherever you are being deployed, please be organized at your roadblock, as your huis deurmekaar is dan val die koppie van die tafel af… (If you’re your house is in a mess, then the cup gets knocked off the table)

(VO) There’s safety in numbers as regulating the roads in Cape Town has become a very dangerous business.

JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town:
We have situations where the staff are assaulted, struck with objects, shot at, bitten, harmed, punched, driven over, dragged by vehicles…. Safety is always a concern.

Derek Piece to Camera:
In Cape Town there is an ongoing stand-off between the authorities and the local taxi industry. It’s a stand-off that can easily explode into violence, claiming lives and causing chaos on commuter routes.

(VO) Taxi protests against police operations on the city’s main arteries often jam traffic, damaging property and putting terrified commuters in harm’s way.

Sequence of arrest of driver
JP Smith: What’s the story, wrong route or no permit?
Officer: No permit at all, sir. And the driver doesn’t have a driver’s licence as well.

(VO) JP Smith is the City politician facing this challenge head on. He’s pushing municipal power to its maximum.

JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town:
We have resorted to increased impoundments as an alternative to fines. we issue 200 to 260,000 fines per month. It doesn't change the behaviour, we've moved our focus to impoundment, it seems to be having more of an impact.

(VO) In Philippi East, disgruntled taxi bosses gather to monitor the roadblocks
(VO) They won’t talk to us but we track down the spokesperson for one of the largest associations here, CATA.

Derek Watts: Nkuleleko, is JP going to improve the situation with his mission?

Nkululeko Sityebi, PRO for CATA, Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association:
JP JP JP JP JP JP JP JP JP.

Derek Watts: Is that a yes or a no?

Nkululeko Sityebi, PRO for CATA, Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association:
It’s a tricky question. If you want to improve it, the initial goal is to engage us. That's simple as that.

(VO) The Western Cape chair of SANTACO says he fears for his industry.

Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO):
Right now it feels like we are being regulated out of existence. It feels like the ultimate goal is to remove our vehicles from the roads,

(VO) But Smith’s patience is running thin.
His office is inundated with complaints that taxi drivers are trying to rule the road at the expense of others.

JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town:
We drew a line in the sand and said we are going to continue this operation because there must be no part of the city that's a no go zone. You need to cut the byte here at no go zone
Visuals of convoy of vehicles driving to the pound at high speed

(VO) But as the city impounds, so elements in the taxi-industry do the same to rivals on the road. It seems that two can play that game, as app-based taxi services have discovered.

Niezaam Azad, Wembley Cabs, E-Hailing Driver:
The taxi industry is obviously a major problem for for us in the e-hailing business…..
they actually get our drivers en route, they take them to the offices and they demand payment, anything between 1000 and 5000 Rand, you know.

(VO) Niezaam Azad has 21 e-hailing vehicles on the road. Five years ago his business was flourishing. Today his drivers are dodging minibus taxis.

Derek Watts: So they act like a police authority?

Niezaam Azad, Wembley Cabs, E-Hailing Driver:
Absolutely. They impound our vehicles because they don't want us on the road. They want all the business. That's that's what they've been doing. And, you know, the police are of no assistance to us.

(VO) This driver was too frightened to reveal his identity. He’s been stopped three times.

Prince: So they asked him Where are these people going? I said they're just going to Delft. And they said haai, No. We've got down to taxis here. And that's four people, that's our money.Then they took all the people from the vehicle.

(VO) Niezaam has set up his own security company to assist when e-hailing companies are under attack

Niezaam Azad, Wembley Cabs, E-Hailing Driver:
You got to put on your bulletproof vests, you got to take your firearm, and get into your car and go and find out what's going on. You know, unfortunately, it's one of those things we need to protect our interest in in the business.
Derek Watts: This is warfare?
Niezaam Azad: Absolutely.

Derek Watts Piece to Camera:
The perceived authority of some associations is daunting. This is from the Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association. We have decided that all the vehicles that transport people in Pollsmoor Prison must stop from the first of October. We will transport them ourselves with our vehicle. Should you not obey to this, we will deal with you as CATA association by impounding your vehicle. Now that is quite a threat.

(VO) Here, the threat was meted out to staff transport, but it’s common BETWEEN associations as well. Industry veteran Jay-Jay Maans says their work environment has changed dramatically over the last decade.

Jay-Jay Maans, Chairman of the Retreat Taxi Association:
Our drivers are being abruptly and rudely stopped and to the extent whereby the keys are taken off and hit and people are being pulled out of the taxis

(VO) He says the trouble came with the arrival of rival associations in the Retreat area. His family have been shot at, and according to him, six drivers murdered with another three surviving shootings. And that’s not counting civilians who got caught in the crossfire. (May have to shorten for Derek’s read)

Jay-Jay Maans, Chairman of the Retreat Taxi Association:
When you went to the Traffics, these people say, eh, you must go to the police. It's a police matter when you go to the police at the time. They told us No, that's a traffic matter. So we didn't go nowhere to go to. We were powerless.

(VO) At the heart of the transport problem is control of routes and passengers. Jay-Jay claims some of their routes have been hijacked by CATA.

Jay Jay Maans, Chairman of the Retreat Taxi Association:
We have the authority our operating licences state that we can go in there. And for 45 years we've been doing it is now four 5 -6 -7 -8 years ago that we've been being stopped.

(VO) CATA denies all these allegations. But Sityebi did concede that not all their members play by the book.

Nkululeko Sityebi, PRO for CATA, Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association:
It's a 80 - 20 situation where the 80 per cent is doing right, and then you find the 20 per cent, they still don't know don't want to open - They don't want to get to understand the nature of the business.

Derek Watts: So there are problems or renegades inside CATA?

Nkululeko Sityebi, PRO for CATA, Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association: That's what I said - it's an 80 - 20 situation.

(VO) SANTACO says the industry is by-and-large law-abiding – but poverty pushes some taxi operators to take chances.

Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO)
And then the violence begins because they they have to finance the purchase of those vehicles, they must pay the banks because now they owe the banks. So those vehicles must work. So they will do everything to ensure that those vehicles are operating, which results in a lot of illegal operators.

(VO) Certainly the bodies pile up. Shoot outs like this one in Camps Bay left three dead, two from the taxi industry, one an innocent bystander. With so few arrests and prosecutions, transport services like Cape Town’s largest commuter bus service, Golden Arrow, operate in a climate of fear.

Derek Watts: I have just seen the scale of this, before the new bylaw - isn’t it a bridge too far, can you cope with this?

JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town:
We must because we must because we cannot afford the number of road deaths we see. We can't afford the level of hostilities and violence that emanates from minibus taxi and other public transport conflict. Can't afford to see Golden Arrow buses burnt out, My Citi buses burnt out trains burnt out

Derek Piece to Camera:
Cape town's largest bus service Golden Arrow declined an interview on who they think might be behind the ongoing attacks on buses and drivers. They've referred us to the Southern African Bus operators Association in Johannesburg, which has a nationwide view of the situation on our roads

Bazil Govender, CEO of the South African Bus Operators Association:
So what are you seeing in Cape Town is symptomatic, again, nationally, okay. It starts with the sporadic attack, then the disruption and then the outright call for suspension of services. But again, what is transpired is that there's been no real entity of face or individual brought to book for us to be able to determine what is behind it.

(VO) In March last year we investigated how Cape Town trains have been destroyed by faceless arsonists.
Up to twelve city commuter buses in Cape Town are attacked in a year.
The mass commuter industry is in trouble but according to government statistics, millions more South Africans are piling into taxis than ever before.

Bazil Govender, CEO of the South African Bus Operators Association:
But between 2013 and current, the bus trajectory went down and the taxi trajectory went up. Taxis currently account for about 82% of daily commute. And it’s not the ideal setup from mass transit,

(VO)Taking a unique hard line in the Cape Metro, Smith wants to bypass the taxi associations altogether. The plan is to ratchet up the pressure by introducing controversial new bylaws. Soon taxi bosses will be penalised for driver’s infringements.

Derek Piece to Camera:
This is where the Cape's taxes are stored after being impounded and when the new bylaw comes into place there's just not going to be enough space to house all the vehicles that the city expect to take off the road

JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town:
The vehicle will remain in the pound for longer, and which will hopefully give more cause for considered driving behaviour and compliance to the drivers.

(VO) At the moment, taxi owners can get their vehicles back on the day of impoundment. But that’s about to change.

Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO):
When you get a fine, your taxi is impounded, you'll get a date to appear in court, which is at least three months from, from the date when you were issued with a ticket. And yet the city is saying on the other side. If after three months, we have not released your vehicle, your vehicle will be sold or crushed, depending on the condition of the vehicle.

Derek Watts: Could there possibly be a violent reaction to the pending bylaws?

Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO):
We hoping not, we are looking at other avenues. Because violence is not going to solve anything. It will just create chaos. And that is not what we want. But we're looking at ways of challenging those aspects of the bylaws that we we feel unfair to the industry. And we will do that through the courts.

(VO)In the meantime, law-enforcers are upping their game, the stakes are high and the sky’s the limit.

JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town:
We do what we can and we're constantly improving our systems. Part of that is better technology, dash cams, body cams for evidentiary purposes, the use of drones, eye in the sky and the use of better legislation to be able to ensure that when we do take an action that the action is impactful and isn't just invalidated or rendered useless by what is now a very frail criminal justice system.


SUNDAY PROMOS AND LINKS

PROMO 1:
We've moved our focus to impoundment, it seems to be having more of an impact.
(VO) High-ways and by-laws – the slow-burn war around mass transport in the Cape is about to get hotter
Their bylaws are simply to criminalise us.

PROMO 2:
(VO) Bringing the taxis to heel….
First of all we have already received information that they are going to attack our vehicles….
(VO) Cape Town’s campaign to lay down the law of the road
….The murderers and killers are still out there.

11 seconds Sound up
(VO) High-ways and by-laws – the slow-burn war around mass transport in the Cape is about to get hotter
Can start this sequence with two cops in car in footage uploaded on Google today PATROL IN VOORTREKKER ROAD - COPS PULL OVERT TAXI - about 10” in puts on siren and cop says Pull over - then bring in JP

It seems that two can play that game, as app-based taxi services have discovered. Niezaam Azad, Wembley Cabs, E-Hailing Driver: The taxi industry is obviously a major problem for for us in the e-hailing business….. they actually get our drivers en route, they take them to the offices and they demand payment, anything between 1000 and 5000 Rand, you know. (VO) Niezaam Azad has 21 e-hailing vehicles on the road. Five years ago his business was flourishing. Today his drivers are dodging minibus taxis. Derek Watts: So they act like a police authority? Niezaam Azad, Wembley Cabs, E-Hailing Driver: Absolutely. They impound our vehicles because they don't want us on the road. They want all the business. That's that's what they've been doing. And, you know, the police are of no assistance to us. (VO) This driver was too frightened to reveal his identity. He’s been stopped three times. Prince: So they asked him Where are these people going? I said they're just going to Delft. And they said haai, No. We've got down to taxis here. And that's four people, that's our money.Then they took all the people from the vehicle. (VO) Niezaam has set up his own security company to assist when e-hailing companies are under attack Niezaam Azad, Wembley Cabs, E-Hailing Driver: You got to put on your bulletproof vests, you got to take your firearm, and get into your car and go and find out what's going on. You know, unfortunately, it's one of those things we need to protect our interest in in the business. Derek Watts: This is warfare? Niezaam Azad: Absolutely. Derek Watts Piece to Camera: The perceived authority of some associations is daunting. This is from the Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association. We have decided that all the vehicles that transport people in Pollsmoor Prison must stop from the first of October. We will transport them ourselves with our vehicle. Should you not obey to this, we will deal with you as CATA association by impounding your vehicle. Now that is quite a threat. (VO) Here, the threat was meted out to staff transport, but it’s common BETWEEN associations as well. Industry veteran Jay-Jay Maans says their work environment has changed dramatically over the last decade. Jay-Jay Maans, Chairman of the Retreat Taxi Association: Our drivers are being abruptly and rudely stopped and to the extent whereby the keys are taken off and hit and people are being pulled out of the taxis (VO) He says the trouble came with the arrival of rival associations in the Retreat area. His family have been shot at, and according to him, six drivers murdered with another three surviving shootings. And that’s not counting civilians who got caught in the crossfire. (May have to shorten for Derek’s read) Jay-Jay Maans, Chairman of the Retreat Taxi Association: When you went to the Traffics, these people say, eh, you must go to the police. It's a police matter when you go to the police at the time. They told us No, that's a traffic matter. So we didn't go nowhere to go to. We were powerless. (VO) At the heart of the transport problem is control of routes and passengers. Jay-Jay claims some of their routes have been hijacked by CATA. Jay Jay Maans, Chairman of the Retreat Taxi Association: We have the authority our operating licences state that we can go in there. And for 45 years we've been doing it is now four 5 -6 -7 -8 years ago that we've been being stopped. (VO) CATA denies all these allegations. But Sityebi did concede that not all their members play by the book. Nkululeko Sityebi, PRO for CATA, Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association: It's a 80 - 20 situation where the 80 per cent is doing right, and then you find the 20 per cent, they still don't know don't want to open - They don't want to get to understand the nature of the business. Derek Watts: So there are problems or renegades inside CATA? Nkululeko Sityebi, PRO for CATA, Cape Amalgamated Taxi Association: That's what I said - it's an 80 - 20 situation. (VO) SANTACO says the industry is by-and-large law-abiding – but poverty pushes some taxi operators to take chances. Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO) And then the violence begins because they they have to finance the purchase of those vehicles, they must pay the banks because now they owe the banks. So those vehicles must work. So they will do everything to ensure that those vehicles are operating, which results in a lot of illegal operators. (VO) Certainly the bodies pile up. Shoot outs like this one in Camps Bay left three dead, two from the taxi industry, one an innocent bystander. With so few arrests and prosecutions, transport services like Cape Town’s largest commuter bus service, Golden Arrow, operate in a climate of fear. Derek Watts: I have just seen the scale of this, before the new bylaw - isn’t it a bridge too far, can you cope with this? JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town: We must because we must because we cannot afford the number of road deaths we see. We can't afford the level of hostilities and violence that emanates from minibus taxi and other public transport conflict. Can't afford to see Golden Arrow buses burnt out, My Citi buses burnt out trains burnt out Derek Piece to Camera: Cape town's largest bus service Golden Arrow declined an interview on who they think might be behind the ongoing attacks on buses and drivers. They've referred us to the Southern African Bus operators Association in Johannesburg, which has a nationwide view of the situation on our roads Bazil Govender, CEO of the South African Bus Operators Association: So what are you seeing in Cape Town is symptomatic, again, nationally, okay. It starts with the sporadic attack, then the disruption and then the outright call for suspension of services. But again, what is transpired is that there's been no real entity of face or individual brought to book for us to be able to determine what is behind it. (VO) In March last year we investigated how Cape Town trains have been destroyed by faceless arsonists. Up to twelve city commuter buses in Cape Town are attacked in a year. The mass commuter industry is in trouble but according to government statistics, millions more South Africans are piling into taxis than ever before. Bazil Govender, CEO of the South African Bus Operators Association: But between 2013 and current, the bus trajectory went down and the taxi trajectory went up. Taxis currently account for about 82% of daily commute. And it’s not the ideal setup from mass transit, (VO)Taking a unique hard line in the Cape Metro, Smith wants to bypass the taxi associations altogether. The plan is to ratchet up the pressure by introducing controversial new bylaws. Soon taxi bosses will be penalised for driver’s infringements. Derek Piece to Camera: This is where the Cape's taxes are stored after being impounded and when the new bylaw comes into place there's just not going to be enough space to house all the vehicles that the city expect to take off the road JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town: The vehicle will remain in the pound for longer, and which will hopefully give more cause for considered driving behaviour and compliance to the drivers. (VO) At the moment, taxi owners can get their vehicles back on the day of impoundment. But that’s about to change. Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO): When you get a fine, your taxi is impounded, you'll get a date to appear in court, which is at least three months from, from the date when you were issued with a ticket. And yet the city is saying on the other side. If after three months, we have not released your vehicle, your vehicle will be sold or crushed, depending on the condition of the vehicle. Derek Watts: Could there possibly be a violent reaction to the pending bylaws? Mandla Hermanus, Western Cape Chair of the South African National Taxi Association (SANTACO): We hoping not, we are looking at other avenues. Because violence is not going to solve anything. It will just create chaos. And that is not what we want. But we're looking at ways of challenging those aspects of the bylaws that we we feel unfair to the industry. And we will do that through the courts. (VO)In the meantime, law-enforcers are upping their game, the stakes are high and the sky’s the limit. JP Smith, Alderman for Safety and Security, City of Cape Town: We do what we can and we're constantly improving our systems. Part of that is better technology, dash cams, body cams for evidentiary purposes, the use of drones, eye in the sky and the use of better legislation to be able to ensure that when we do take an action that the action is impactful and isn't just invalidated or rendered useless by what is now a very frail criminal justice system. SUNDAY PROMOS AND LINKS PROMO 1: We've moved our focus to impoundment, it seems to be having more of an impact. (VO) High-ways and by-laws – the slow-burn war around mass transport in the Cape is about to get hotter Their bylaws are simply to criminalise us. PROMO 2: (VO) Bringing the taxis to heel…. First of all we have already received information that they are going to attack our vehicles…. (VO) Cape Town’s campaign to lay down the law of the road ….The murderers and killers are still out there. 11 seconds Sound up (VO) High-ways and by-laws – the slow-burn war around mass transport in the Cape is about to get hotter Can start this sequence with two cops in car in footage uploaded on Google today PATROL IN VOORTREKKER ROAD - COPS PULL OVERT TAXI - about 10” in puts on siren and cop says Pull over - then bring in JP

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ..we probe the conflict points in a faceless war on public transport in Cape Town
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have footage of taxis being impounded in what is arguably the most concentrated and largest law enforcement effort by traffic police in Cape Town to date, setting the scene for a more difficult relationship between the state and the taxi associations who are both operating in a compromised and broken public transport sector. We also will have interview with newly appoint SANTACO provincial head who is attempting to build bridges while on the ground his operators break the rules. As an example of that, we show a case study of an e-hailing entrepreneur whose drivers are regularly stopped by taxi-drivers on a mission to confiscate the cars of competition, or levy a fine, and a letter to transport business owners operating transport from Pollsmoor from CATA threatening to do exactly that in the Tokai area.
metadata.Summary: Public transport related violence flares up monthly in Cape Town, hurting the local economy, undermining freedom of movement on a mass scaled, hurting private and public property and most of all claiming lives. The word on the street is that the taxi associations and operators are intent on driving other forms of public transport off the road - trains, buses, e-hailing, staff and school transport - using violence, intimidation and lawlessness. Now the city is to ratchet up the tension in this low-scale war by introducing a new and unique to the Cape bylaw which will hit the operators where it hurts - in their pockets - while it sets itself up to impound taxi's on an almost industrial scale and not give them back on the same day. In this instance, the Cape is a case-study of extremes, but the head of the Bus Operators Organisation explains that similar scenarios are playing out across the country and we ignore this encroachment at our peril.
metadata.Further information: We will do the interview with Councillor JP Smith, the man leading the state in this low-scale war of regulatory aggression against the taxi sector in the City's pound which is bursting at the scenes with impounded taxis. Beyond the interview, this will give us unique visuals. We also will have access to some of the City's footage of taxi violence.
